newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesian markets weaken, rupiah plunges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesian markets weaken, rupiah plunges.

text.p: Indonesia's markets went through another harrowing session on Wednesday with the rupiah plunging to a record low before recovering on central bank intervention and the stock market closing markedly weaker.

The fallout from continuing weakness in South East Asian currencies drove the rupiah to a historic low against the dollar for the second time in four weeks, forcing Bank Indonesia to intervene in the market, dealers said.

The Jakarta stock market composite index closed down 0.66 percent at 658.60 points in response to the weaker currency and higher interest rates announced by Bank Indonesia in a vain bid to stem currency speculation, brokers said.
The index has fallen by more than 50 points since the beginning of the month on a combination of high interest rates, new controls on margin finance and a slew of rights issues.
The rupiah fell to a low of 2,682 to the dollar in the afternoon despite the higher rates before recovering on the intervention to 2,650/80.

The bank's intervention band, the parameters outside of which it will enter the market, was maintained at 2,378/2,682 at the daily fixing, indicating authorities were not immediately considering any change in policy.

There was no indication of how much money the bank had pumped into the market. Analysts said it could well be a losing battle given the continuing weakness in all South East Asian currencies and their susceptibility to contagion.

"It's useless for the central bank to intervene in a bearish market," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist for the I.D.E.A. research consultancy. He noted that the Malaysian central bank had spent some $8.8 billion in intervention measures when the ringgit was under attack earlier this month, but with little to show for its efforts.

The ringgit slumped to a 42-month low of 2.7930 against the dollar on Tuesday and continued to be weak on Wednesday. Its weakness has spread to Indonesia, compounding earlier contagion from the Thai baht, analysts said.

"First it was the tom yam effect," said Koh. "Now it's the asam laksa effect," referring to a fiery Thai soup and popular Malaysian noodles-in-soup dish. The fallout from currency turmoil in Thailand and Malaysia has hit all regional markets.

Earlier, Bank Indonesia raised interest rates for central bank certificates of all maturities by 100 basis points. The move makes it more expensive for investors to borrow rupiah, which could then be used for speculation.
But Koh said the raising of rates could only be used as a short-term measure and forecast a further fall in the rupiah as domestic corporates began to hedge their currency risks.
"Corporates here are not used to hedging risk, but with things the way they are, they have no option," Koh said. "That will affect the rupiah further."
Dealers in Jakarta said the contagion effect was exacerbated by a newspaper report quoting a leading local economist as saying that the rupiah should be allowed to find its own level.
Sjahrir, an economist and brokerage firm owner, told the Kompas daily that Bank Indonesia need not intervene and that the market would ultimately decide a fair value for the rupiah.

"According to me, just let the rupiah fall to 2,700 or 2,800. The central bank does not have to do anything. Once they (speculators) realise the central bank hasn't done anything, the dollar is already overvalued," Sjahrir was quoted as saying.
The rupiah's previous historic low was 2,665 on July 21.
Donald Hanna, an economist with Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong, said raising interest rates was however a sensible move to curb the rupiah volatility.
"The economy is not as weak as in Thailand," he said. "There is more resilience to higher interest rates. There is no fundamental reason for the rupiah to weaken."
